latin.1694: I. Communis Ecclesiae Romanae Doctrina est, primum hominem, antequam Diabolo instigante peccaret, praeditum fuisse vera justitia & sanctitate, cujus respectu Deo gratus & acceptus erat ad vitam aeternam. Id manifeste docet Concilium ipsum Tridentinum Sessione quinta decreto De peccato Originali. Ubi anathema dicit, illi qui non confitetur primum hominem Adam, cum mandatum Dei in paradiso fuisset transgressus, statim sanctitatem & justitiam in qua constitutus fuerat amisisse. Et praeterea illi qui asserit Adamum acceptam a Deo sanctitatem & justitiam quam perdidit, sibi soli, & non nobis etiam perdidisse.
latin.1695: II. Porro justitia & sanctitas illa, ex mente Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, non in eo solum consistebat, quod mens hominis imbuta erat vera Dei cognitione, & quae ad aeternae beatitudinis adeptionem sufficeret; ejus vero voluntas puro & casto amore Deum complectebatur: sed praeterea in eo quod caro spiritui, & corpus animae sine difficultate & repugnantia parebat, & appetitus sensitivus ita rationis ductum sequebatur, ut adversus eam nunquam rebellaret, & in diversa hominem traheret: ac proinde Adam in illo integritatis statu nullam in se luctam carnis & spiritus, nullamque membrorum adversus legem mentis rebellionem, qualem frequenter in nobis sentimus, experiretur: sed ad bonum ferretur, & a malo sese averteret sine pugna & difficultate, neque haberet in se praedictam illam concupiscentiam, cum qua jam nascimur, & quae usque ad mortem in nobis perseverat.
latin.1696: III. Quaeritur autem an ista justitia & sanctitas primo homini fuerit naturalis, necne? Ad quam quaestionem ut respondeant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, observant naturale variis modis sumi. Primo enim naturale dicitur omne quod habetur a nativitate: & ita naturale opponitur adventitio. Secundo naturale vocatur illud quod est naturae consentaneum, quodque naturam non destruit, sed potius ornat & perficit. Quo sensu naturale opponitur ei quod est contra naturam. Tertio naturale vocatur quod aut est pars naturae, aut fluit ex principiis naturae, vel ab illis fluere aptum est. Qua significatione corpus & animus, facultates quoque tum sentiendi, tum intelligendi, & operationes quae ab eis facultatibus, absque auxilio naturam superante exercentur, naturalia dicuntur: & ita naturale opponitur supernaturali.
latin.1697: IV. Jam vero nonnulli sunt inter Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui justitiam & sanctitatem illam, quae, fatente tota Ecclesia Romana, in primis parentibus ante peccatum reperiebatur, pertendant naturalem modis omnibus fuisse, & non solum quatenus naturale distinguitur ab adventitio, sive ab eo quod est contra naturam; sed etiam quatenus opponitur supernaturali. Nec enim justitiam illam fuisse gratiam supernaturalem, sed ad naturalem hominis nondum corrupti statum pertinuisse, & fuisse conditionem naturae integrae debitam. Id testatur Medina in 1. 2. quaest. 18. articulo 2. Intelligunt, inquit, Doctores quidam per hominem constitutum in puris naturalibus hominem constitutum in natura integra, cum dono & vigore sanante naturam, adeo ut in bono & officio virtutum posset permanere, & perseverare si vellet; Quae sententia sine dubio videtur esse Augustini. Et hi sunt viri illi insigniter eruditi, qui, teste Bellarmino, censent idem sensisse Thomam ipsum cum caeteris authoribus probatioribus, & eos hac in parte contrarium tenuisse ejus quod Bellarminus ipse docet.
latin.1698: V. Verum haec sententia fuit a Pontificibus Romanis videlicet, Pio V. & Gregorio XIII. superiori saeculo damnata. Nam inter multos articulos in singulari Bulla horum Pontificum damnatos, iste est vigesimus primus. Humanae naturae sublimatio, & exaltatio in consortium divinae debita fuit integritati primae conditionis, ac proinde naturalis dicenda est, non supernaturalis. Sextus vero & vigesimus his verbis conceptus est, Integritas primae conditionis non fuit indebita humanae naturae exaltatio, sed ejus naturalis conditio. Ut refert Bellarminus de gratia primi hominis, lib. unico, cap. 1.
latin.1699: VI. Itaque Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae communis sententia est, justitiam & sanctitatem, qua primus homo ante lapsum ornatus erat, naturalem quidem dici posse, quatenus naturale opponitur ei quod est contra naturam, & significat id quod est naturae consentaneum, & quod naturam non destruit, sed ornat & perficit: aut etiam quatenus naturale opponitur ei quod est adventitium, & significat id quod inest ab origine, seu a nativitate. Admittunt enim primum nostrum parentem in justitia fuisse creatum: & idcirco justitiam illam, qua in integritatis statu praeditus erat, vocant Originalem. Sed negant istam justitiam fuisse naturalem, quatenus naturale opponitur supernaturali; quia scilicet, ex eorum mente, ex principiis naturae non fluxit, sed fuit donum Dei gratuitum, quod hominem supra naturalem conditionem evexit.
latin.1700: VII. Ut autem hac in parte mentem suam clarius explicent, observant aliquid supernaturale dici duobus modis, per se & per accidens. Per se dicitur supernaturale, quod ex genere suo non est aptum fluere ex principiis naturae: qualis fuit ascensus Eliae igneo curru in coelum, robur Sampsonis, & alia id genus. Per accidens supernaturale vocatur quod interdum obtinetur divino miraculo, licet alioquin ex naturae principiis fluere soleat. Talis fuit sensus videndi quem Dominus caeco nato restituit: sapientia Salomoni divinitus tributa, & alia non pauca quae in scripturis leguntur.
latin.1701: VIII. Jam autem justitiae donum in primo homine volunt supernaturale fuisse, non tantum per accidens, quia nimirum fuerit gratis & immediate, & modo quodam naturam superante a Deo collatum: sed etiam per se, & ex suo genere quia justitia illa quae primum hominem ornabat nec fluxit, nec fluere potuit ex principiis naturae etiam non corruptae. Nec enim posse hominem, etiam nondum peccato infectum, propriis naturae viribus Deum & nosse & amare, quantum requirit justitia & sanctitas Deo grata & accepta, ad vitae & beatitudinis aeternae praemium. Neque etiam per solas vires & dona naturae posse corpus animae, sensumque & appetitum rationi ita perfecte subjici; ut nulla in homine existat carnis adversus spiritum rebellio, neque ullam in bene agendo difficultatem & repugnantiam, aut ad male agendum proclivitatem in se experiatur, sicuti res in homine integro se habebat, in quo scilicet nulli erant inordinati, & adversus rectam rationem rebelles concupiscentiae motus.
latin.1702: IX. Haec est doctrina Bellarmini de gratia primi hominis libro unico, cap. 4. Ubi haec est ejus quarta propositio, Rectitudo illa cum qua Adamus creatus fuit, & sine qua post ejus lapsum omnes homines nascuntur, donum supernaturale fuit. Quam propositionem ut explicet, observat primo hominem naturaliter constare ex carne & spiritu, & ideo partim cum bestiis, partim cum Angelis communicare naturam: & quidem ratione carnis & communionis cum bestiis, habere propensionem quandam ad bonum corporale & sensibile, in quod fertur per sensum & appetitum: ratione vero spiritus & communionis cum Angelis, habere propensionem ad bonum spirituale & intelligibile, in quod fertur per intelligentiam & voluntatem. Ex his autem diversis vel contrariis propensionibus existere in uno eodemque homine pugnam quandam & ex ea pugna ingentem bene agendi difficultatem, dum una propensio alteram impedit.
latin.1703: X. Deinde dicit divinam providentiam initio creationis, ut remedium adhiberet huic morbo seu languori naturae humanae, qui ex conditione materiae oriebatur, addidisse homini donum quoddam insigne, justitiam videlicet Originalem, qua veluti aureo quodam fraeno pars inferior parti superiori, & pars superior Deo facile subjecta contineretur. Sic autem subjectam carnem spiritui, ut non posset ipso invito moveri, neque ei rebellis fieri, nisi ipse fieret rebellis Deo; in potestate tamen spiritus fuisse Deo rebellem fieri, & non fieri. Unde colligit primi hominis justitiam naturalem quidem fuisse, quatenus naturale dicitur id omne quod habetur a nativitate, & quatenus naturale dicitur id quod est naturae consentaneum, sed non fuisse naturalem, quatenus naturale distinguitur a supernaturali, & significat id quod fluit ex principiis naturae.
latin.1704: XI. Adversarii, inquit, censent rectitudinem illam in qua creatus est Adam fuisse illi naturalem hoc ultimo modo (nempe quatenus naturale opponitur supernaturali) nimirum quod fuerit veluti quaedam sanitas debita naturae, aptaque nasci ex ipsa natura bene constituta, id est, non corrupta: & nunc hominibus qui eam rectitudinem amiserunt in Adamo, deesse bonum aliquod naturale, quale deesse pecudi, si caeca, vel claudicans, vel febricitans nasceretur. Et nunc, si alicui homini originalis illa justitia divinitus redderetur, dicerent esse donum supernaturale per accidens, non per se, ut diximus de oculis redditis caeco nato. Nos vero existimamus rectitudinem illam, etiam partis inferioris, fuisse donum supernaturale, & quidem per se, non per accidens, ita ut neque ex principiis naturae fluxerit, neque potuerit fluere. Et quia donum illud supernaturale erat, ut statim probaturi sumus, eo remoto, natura humana sibi relicta pugnam illam experiri coepit partis inferioris cum superiore, quae naturalis futura erat, id est, ex conditione materiae sequutura, nisi Deus justitiae donum homini addidisset. Quare non magis differt status hominis post lapsum Adae, a statu ejusdem in puris naturalibus, quam differt spoliatus a nudo: neque deterior est humana natura, si culpam originalem detrahas, neque magis ignorantia & infirmitate laborat, quam esset & laboraret in puris naturalibus condita. Proinde corruptio naturae non ex alicujus doni naturalis carentia, neque ex alicujus malae qualitatis accessu, sed ex sola doni supernaturalis ob Adae peccatum amissione profluxit. Quam sententiam communem esse Doctorum Scholasticorum veterum & recentiorum, multis postea allatis eorum testimoniis probat.
latin.1705: XII. Sed quamvis Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae in eo communiter hodie consentiant quod justitia & sanctitas hominis in integritatis & innocentiae statu fuit donum quoddam supernaturale, & gratia proprie sic dicta ac naturae superaddita: inter eos tamen hic restat sententiarum notabile discrimen. Etenim eorum nonnulli justitiam & sanctitatem primi hominis sic volunt fuisse supernaturalem, & ad gratiam non ad naturam pertinuisse, ut fuerit tamen quodammodo innocenti naturae debita. Ita ut impossibile fuerit primum hominem sine tali gratia a Deo condi & creari: quia scilicet, hoc repugnavisset divinae bonitati, justitiae, & sapientiae. Alioquin enim futurum fuisse, ut Deus crearet hominem vel malum, vel miserum, aut potius utrumque. Nam non potest non malus & non miser non esse qui Deum nec novit, nec amat puro & casto amore, prout creaturam rationalem decet: & in quo corporei sensus & appetitus rationem invitam & renitentem trahunt ad haec inferiora, nec mentis imperiis & dictamini parent, sed adversus eam rebellant atque tumultuantur. Est autem bonitati divinae contrarium, ut condat hominem malum & peccatorem, aut saltem miserum, absque ulla ipsius culpa.
latin.1706: XIII. Itaque non existimant debitum omne cum gratia pugnare, sed solum illud quod in bonis operibus & meritis fundatur. Proinde quamvis Deus, dum creaturam rationalem condit, debeat, id exigente bonitate, & sapientia ejus, ei dona conferre, & auxilia praebere quae necessaria sunt ad Deum puro & casto amore prosequendum, vitamque justam tranquillam & beatam degendam, dona & auxilia ista nihilominus, ex eorum mente, non ad naturam, sed ad gratiam proprie dictam pertinent: quoniam talia dona & auxilia nullo modo meritis creaturae debentur, & creatura ex se ad ista non sufficit, nisi supra naturam a Deo adjuvetur.
latin.1707: XIV. Haec est doctrina eorum qui Jansenii doctrinam & placita sequuntur, ut videre est in brevi Catechismo quem de gratia ediderunt. Ibi enim capite quarto, postquam asseruerunt primum hominem fuisse creatum in statu sanctitatis & justitiae, cognitionis & amoris divini, Deo simul naturam formante, & gratiam communicante, docent hominem in alio statu creari non potuisse: quoniam Deus nihil facere potest quod ordinatum non sit: jam vero creaturam rationalem inordinatam fore, nisi in statu gratiae crearetur. Id autem ita esse probant ex eo, quod creaturae intellectualis ordo essentialis est, ut ad Deum tendat tanquam ad centrum suum, & originem suam. Illuc autem tendere non potest, nisi per auxilium quod gratia subministrat. Unde sequitur creaturam talem futuram extra proprium ordinem, si nondum peccato corrupta, gratia privaretur.
latin.1708: XV. Ista petita sunt ex Jansenio ipso qui in libro posthumo, qui Augustinus inscribitur, prolixe doctrinam eandem ex Augustino colligit, probat, & amplificat. Praecipue vero primo & secundo libro de statu naturae purae, ubi multis argumentis confirmat & ostendit hominem non potuisse in statu naturae purae, sine omni gratia creari: quia per solas naturae, etiam non corruptae vires, absque gratiae naturam adjuvantis auxilio, nequit homo Deum ullo vero amore diligere, & ulla qualicunque Dei contemplatione & fruitione beari. Adeoque si Deus supponeretur hominem in statu naturae purae, sine omni gratia creare, necessario illum crearet & malum & miserum: quod Dei bonitati & sapientiae omnino repugnat. Ac praeterea docet gratiam dilectionis Dei, in qua primus homo creatus est, verissimam retinere rationem gratiae, quamvis Deus eam nullo justitiae debito, sed ex condecentia infirmitatis creaturae, ex lege suae sapientiae, suaeque benignitatis, & sanctitatis, & misericordiae propriaeque rectitudinis, creaturae innocenti largiatur, ne alioquin omnia peccata, & dilectio ejus in inferiora diffluens, in ipsum revolvantur Deum, qui ei dilectionem ex nemine nisi ex Deo principio & fine suo religare praecepit. Quae sunt ipsa Jansenii verba, lib. 1. de statu naturae, cap. 20. cujus titulus est, Quomodo Bona voluntas, in qua condi debet creatura rationalis, esset gratia.
latin.1709: XVI. Nam ut ibidem videre est, ex ejus sententia, gratiae etiam propriissime dictae non repugnant debita quaelibet, seu connaturalitates, decentiae, congruentiae & aequitates, quae oriuntur ex aliis capitibus, quam ex jure creaturae. Ideoque quamvis nihil connaturalius fuerit creaturae ad imaginem Dei conditae, quam ut cum Dei notitia & amore crearetur: nihilque congruentius, decentius & aequius respectu Dei fuerit, quam ut rationali creaturae innocenti, quae ad Deum velut finem suum naturalem ordinata est, ea darentur quae ad assequendum finem illum necessaria sunt, idque Deus sibi ipsi, suisque attributis quodammodo deberet: attamen illa Dei cognitio atque dilectio, sine qua Deo frui nulla creatura potest, gratia dici meretur, etiam creaturarum innocentium respectu; tum quia nullis meritis creaturae debetur, tum quia cognitio & dilectio hujusmodi naturae cujuscunque creatae vires superat, nisi supra naturam a Deo adjuvetur.
latin.1710: XVII. Sed in diversum abit communior Doctorum Scholae Romanae sententia. Etenim existimant justitiam & sanctitatem, quae in primo homine fuit, non solum fuisse donum supernaturale, & quod ad naturam non ad gratiam pertinebat; sed etiam aliquid naturae humanae, quamvis innocenti & nondum peccatrici, prorsus indebitum: ita ut nihil repugnaret sapientiae, bonitati, & justitiae divinae hominem sine tali justitia creari. Unde est quod inter status hominis possibiles ponunt statum purae naturae, sive hominis, ut loquuntur, in puris naturalibus. In quo statu ex eorum mente, homo nec justus, nec injustus esset: nec ullius peccati reus nec etiam ulla gratia praeditus.
latin.1711: XVIII. Nam ut mentem Scholasticorum hac in parte refert & explicat jam dictus Jansenius, de statu naturae purae libro primo capite primo, juxta illos, pura natura dicitur puritate negativa, quia scilicet, nihil habet superadditum sive bonum, sive malum, quod ei debitum non sit: ita neque peccatum habeat, poenamque peccati comitem, neque ullum gratiae naturam superantis donum.
latin.1712: XIX. Ut vero facile intelligatur, quid hujusmodi naturae status comprehendat, naturam lapsam intueri jubent, in qua quicquid praeter peccati reatum deprehendimus, hoc ad puram naturam pertinere profitentur. Quippe Regula solennis eorum est, naturam puram a natura lapsa discrepare sicut nudum a spoliato, qui non aliter differunt, nisi quod hic amiserit, quod alter nunquam habuit: ut proinde pura natura se habeat instar negationis, lapsa instar privationis.
latin.1713: XX. Itaque quum docent hominem a Deo creari posse, nullo omnino praecedente peccato, in statu naturae purae, id sibi volunt hominem eo casu creandum esse sine ordinatione ad beatitudinem sempiternam, seu claram visionem Dei, & consequenter sine fide in intellectu, & sine charitate Deum diligente condendum. Praeterea repugnantiam illam carnis & spiritus, quam in nobis experimur, tali homini fore prorsus naturalem. Usque adeo ut ordo mere naturalis postulet, ut Deus duos illos appetitus contrarios reciprocis motibus conflictari sinat, neque concursum suum subtrahendo, neque dono quopiam superaddito mutuam pugnam hostilitatemque comprimendo.
latin.1714: XXI. Ac proinde quantum ad internas animi vires, tantam in pura natura futuram ignorantiam, beneque cogitandi, judicandi, & vivendi infirmitatem, peccandique pronitatem, quantam in natura lapsa experimur. Quantum ad externa vero majorem. Nam praeterquam quod objecta sensibilia concupiscentiam excitantia essent eadem, mala pravorum hominum consilia, & exempla potentius tunc ad malum provocarent. Nam cognitio Dei virtutumque quae Adamo communicata fuerat, & memoria promissionum & comminationum Dei, priorisque status & praeteriti lapsus recordatio, & promissio venturi Christi, cum spe redemptionis ejus, quae per traditionem a capite in posteros diffusa promanarunt; peccandi facilitatem in natura lapsa mitigare potuerunt, ut hac in parte caecitas, corruptio morum generalior, peccandique pronitas in pura natura proclivior futura fuisse videatur.

sections.title: Rome's common teaching: Adam before the fall had true righteousness and holiness (Trent, Session 5)
sections.pass_a: The common Doctrine of the Roman Church is that the first man, before he sinned at the Devil's instigation, was endowed with true justice and sanctity, in respect of which he was pleasing and accepted to God for eternal life. The Council of Trent itself plainly teaches this in the fifth Session, in the decree On Original sin. Where it says anathema to him who does not confess that the first man Adam, when he had transgressed the command of God in paradise, immediately lost the sanctity and justice in which he had been constituted. And moreover to him who asserts that Adam lost the sanctity and justice received from God, which he lost, for himself alone, and not for us also.
pass_b: The common teaching of the Roman Church is that the first man, before he sinned at the devil's prompting, was endowed with true righteousness and holiness, on account of which he was pleasing and acceptable to God for eternal life.

The Council of Trent itself teaches this plainly in its fifth session, in the decree on original sin. There it pronounces anathema on anyone who does not confess that the first man, Adam, when he had broken God's command in paradise, at once lost the holiness and righteousness in which he had been placed. It pronounces it too on anyone who asserts that the holiness and righteousness Adam received from God and then lost, he lost for himself alone and not for us as well.

choices.why: Justitia here is the original righteousness of Adam, so 'righteousness' rather than the forensic or civic 'justice'.

notes: Trent, Session 5 (1546), Decree on Original Sin, canons 1 and 2. The command in paradise is that of Genesis 2:16-17; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: What that righteousness included: true knowledge and pure love of God, and a body and appetite obeying the spirit without struggle
sections.pass_a: Further, that justice and sanctity, in the mind of the Doctors of the Roman Church, did not consist only in this, that the mind of man was imbued with true knowledge of God, and such as would suffice for the attainment of eternal blessedness; and his will embraced God with pure and chaste love: but besides in this, that the flesh obeyed the spirit, and the body the soul, without difficulty and repugnance, and the sensitive appetite so followed the leading of reason that it never rebelled against it, and drew man in different directions: and therefore Adam in that state of integrity experienced in himself no struggle of flesh and spirit, and no rebellion of the members against the law of the mind, such as we often feel in ourselves: but was borne to good, and turned himself from evil without fight and difficulty, nor had in himself that aforesaid concupiscence, with which we are now born, and which persists in us until death.
pass_b: In the view of the Roman Church's teachers, that righteousness and holiness did not consist only in man's mind being filled with a true knowledge of God, enough for gaining eternal blessedness, and in his will embracing God with pure and chaste love.

It also consisted in this: the flesh obeyed the spirit and the body the soul without difficulty or resistance, and the sensual appetite followed reason's lead so fully that it never rebelled against it or pulled the man in different directions.

So Adam in that unfallen state felt within himself no struggle of flesh against spirit, and no rebellion of his members against the law of his mind, such as we often feel. He moved toward good and turned away from evil without conflict or difficulty, and he did not have in him the concupiscence spoken of above, with which we are now born and which stays with us until death.

choices.english: rebellion of his members against the law of his mind
choices.why: Le Blanc's phrase is Paul's in Romans 7:23; the English keeps the Pauline wording.

notes: The law of the members against the law of the mind is from Romans 7:23, and the struggle of flesh and spirit echoes Galatians 5:17; the print gives no references.

sections.title: Was it natural? Rome's three senses of natural: from birth, agreeable to nature, flowing from nature's principles
sections.pass_a: But it is asked whether that justice and sanctity was natural to the first man, or not? To answer this question the Doctors of the Roman Church observe that natural is taken in various ways. For first natural is called everything which is had from birth: and so natural is opposed to adventitious. Second that is called natural which is agreeable to nature, and which does not destroy nature, but rather adorns and perfects it. In which sense natural is opposed to that which is against nature. Third that is called natural which either is part of nature, or flows from the principles of nature, or is apt to flow from them. In which signification body and soul, also the faculties both of sensing and of understanding, and the operations which are exercised by those faculties without aid surpassing nature, are called natural: and so natural is opposed to supernatural.
pass_b: The question is whether this righteousness and holiness was natural to the first man or not. To answer it, the teachers of the Roman Church point out that "natural" is used in several ways.

First, whatever one has from birth is called natural, and in this sense natural is opposed to acquired. Second, what suits nature, what does not destroy nature but rather adorns and perfects it, is called natural; in this sense natural is opposed to what is against nature.

Third, what is either a part of nature, or flows from nature's principles, or is fitted to flow from them, is called natural. In this sense the body and the soul, the powers of sense and of understanding, and the acts those powers perform without help that goes beyond nature, are called natural, and so natural is opposed to supernatural.

choices.why: Adventitium is what comes to a thing from outside after its origin; 'acquired' carries that in plain English.

sections.title: Some Roman doctors held it natural in every sense, even as opposed to supernatural (Medina)
sections.pass_a: But now there are some among the Doctors of the Roman Church who maintain that that justice and sanctity, which, as the whole Roman Church admits, was found in the first parents before sin, was natural in all ways, and not only insofar as natural is distinguished from adventitious, or from that which is against nature; but also insofar as it is opposed to supernatural. For that justice was not supernatural grace, but pertained to the natural state of man not yet corrupted, and was a condition owed to integral nature. Medina testifies to this on 1. 2. question 18. article 2. Certain Doctors, he says, understand by man constituted in pure naturals man constituted in integral nature, with a gift and vigor healing nature, so that he could remain in the good and duty of the virtues, and persevere if he wished; Which opinion without doubt seems to be Augustine's. And these are those notably learned men, who, by Bellarmine's witness, think that Thomas himself thought the same with the other more approved authors, and that they held in this part the contrary of what Bellarmine himself teaches.
pass_b: Some teachers of the Roman Church, however, maintain that the righteousness and holiness which the whole Roman Church agrees was found in our first parents before sin was natural in every sense. It was natural, they say, not only as natural is distinguished from acquired or from what is against nature, but also as it is opposed to supernatural. That righteousness was not supernatural grace; it belonged to the natural state of man not yet corrupted, and was a condition owed to unfallen nature.

Medina bears witness to this on the Prima Secundae, question 18, article 2: "Some teachers understand by 'man placed in a purely natural state' man placed in unfallen nature, with a gift and strength that heals nature, so that he could remain in the good and in the practice of the virtues and persevere if he chose. This opinion is without doubt Augustine's."

These are the remarkably learned men who, as Bellarmine reports, think that Thomas himself held the same view along with the other more reputable authors, and that on this point they held the opposite of what Bellarmine himself teaches.

choices.why: The scholastic technical phrase for man with nature only and no added gift; the English keeps it recognizable without Latin.

notes: Bartolomé de Medina (1527-1580), Dominican commentator on Thomas Aquinas' Summa, Prima Secundae.

sections.title: That view condemned by Pius V and Gregory XIII (Baius' articles 21 and 26)
sections.pass_a: But this opinion was condemned by the Roman Pontiffs, namely, Pius V. and Gregory XIII. in the last century. For among the many articles condemned in a singular Bull of these Pontiffs, this is the twenty-first. The sublimation and exaltation of human nature into the fellowship of the divine was owed to the integrity of the first condition, and therefore must be called natural, not supernatural. But the twenty-sixth is conceived in these words, The integrity of the first condition was not an unowed exaltation of human nature, but its natural condition. As Bellarmine reports on the grace of the first man, sole book, chap. 1.
pass_b: Popes Pius V and Gregory XIII condemned this view in the last century. In their bull, which condemned many articles together, it appears as article 21: "Human nature's being lifted up and raised into partnership with the divine nature was owed to the integrity of man's first condition, and is therefore to be called natural, not supernatural."

Article 26 runs: "The integrity of man's first condition was not an exaltation of human nature beyond its due, but its natural condition." Bellarmine records this in chapter 1 of his single book On the Grace of the First Man.

choices.english: into partnership with the divine nature
choices.why: Consortium divinae (naturae) recalls 2 Peter 1:4, 'partakers of the divine nature'.

notes: The articles are from the propositions of Michael Baius condemned by Pius V (Ex omnibus afflictionibus, 1567) and again by Gregory XIII (1579). 'Partnership with the divine nature' echoes 2 Peter 1:4; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: So Rome's common view: natural as agreeable to nature and as present from origin, but not as opposed to supernatural
sections.pass_a: Therefore the common opinion of the Doctors of the Roman Church is that the justice and sanctity with which the first man before the fall was adorned can indeed be called natural, insofar as natural is opposed to that which is against nature, and signifies what is agreeable to nature, and which does not destroy nature, but adorns and perfects it: or also insofar as natural is opposed to what is adventitious, and signifies what is present from origin, or from birth. For they admit that our first parent was created in justice: and therefore they call that justice, with which he was endowed in the state of integrity, Original. But they deny that this justice was natural, insofar as natural is opposed to supernatural; because namely, in their mind, it did not flow from the principles of nature, but was a gratuitous gift of God, which raised man above his natural condition.
pass_b: The common view of the Roman Church's teachers, then, is that the righteousness and holiness with which the first man was adorned before the fall can indeed be called natural in two senses. It is natural as opposed to what is against nature, meaning what suits nature and does not destroy it but adorns and perfects it. It is natural too as opposed to what is acquired, meaning what is there from the origin, or from birth.

For they grant that our first parent was created in righteousness, and so they call the righteousness he had in his unfallen state original righteousness. But they deny that it was natural as natural is opposed to supernatural, because in their view it did not flow from nature's principles but was God's free gift, which raised man above his natural condition.

choices.why: The gift lifts man above his natural level; 'raised' keeps the image without overstatement.

sections.title: Supernatural per se and per accidens: Elijah's chariot and Samson's strength; the blind man's sight and Solomon's wisdom
sections.pass_a: But that they may explain their mind more clearly in this part, they observe that something is called supernatural in two ways, per se and per accidens. That is called supernatural per se which of its own kind is not apt to flow from the principles of nature: such was the ascent of Elijah in a fiery chariot into heaven, the strength of Samson, and other things of that kind. That is called supernatural per accidens which is sometimes obtained by divine miracle, although otherwise it is wont to flow from the principles of nature. Such was the sense of seeing which the Lord restored to the man born blind: the wisdom divinely bestowed on Solomon, and not a few other things which are read in the scriptures.
pass_b: To make their meaning clearer on this point, they note that something is called supernatural in two ways, in itself (per se) and by circumstance (per accidens).

What by its very kind is not fitted to flow from nature's principles is supernatural in itself, like Elijah's going up to heaven in a fiery chariot, Samson's strength, and other things of that sort. What is sometimes obtained by a divine miracle, though otherwise it usually flows from nature's principles, is supernatural by circumstance. Such was the sight the Lord gave back to the man born blind, the wisdom God gave Solomon, and many other things we read in Scripture.

choices.why: The scholastic pair is kept in Latin once and glossed so the later theses read plainly.

notes: The examples are Elijah (2 Kings 2:11), Samson (Judges 14-16), the man born blind (John 9) and Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 3:12); the print gives no references.

sections.title: Rome holds original righteousness supernatural in itself: unfallen nature could not by its own powers so know and love God, or so rule the body
sections.pass_a: But now they hold that the gift of justice in the first man was supernatural, not only per accidens, because namely it was conferred by God freely and immediately, and in a certain manner surpassing nature: but also per se, and of its own kind because that justice which adorned the first man neither flowed, nor could flow, from the principles of nature even not corrupted. For man, even not yet infected with sin, cannot by the proper powers of nature both know and love God, as much as the justice and sanctity pleasing and accepted by God requires, for the reward of eternal life and blessedness. Nor also by the powers and gifts of nature alone can the body be subjected to the soul, and sense and appetite to reason, so perfectly; that no rebellion of the flesh against the spirit exists in man, nor he experience in himself any difficulty and repugnance in acting well, or proneness to acting badly, as the matter stood in integral man, in whom namely there were no inordinate motions of concupiscence, rebellious against right reason.
pass_b: They hold, then, that the gift of righteousness in the first man was supernatural not only by circumstance, because God gave it freely, directly and in a way beyond nature, but also in itself and by its kind, because the righteousness that adorned the first man neither flowed nor could flow from nature's principles, even uncorrupted nature.

Man, even before sin had infected him, could not by nature's own powers know and love God as fully as a righteousness and holiness that pleases God and is accepted by him requires for the reward of eternal life and blessedness.

Nor could nature's powers and gifts alone subject body to soul, and sense and appetite to reason, so perfectly that there was no rebellion of flesh against spirit in man, and that he felt no difficulty or resistance in doing good and no leaning toward doing evil. Yet that is how things stood in unfallen man, in whom there were no disordered movements of concupiscence rebelling against right reason.

choices.why: The point is that even unfallen nature lacked this power; the English keeps the 'even'.

sections.title: Bellarmine's fourth proposition: Adam's rectitude was a supernatural gift; man's two propensions, from flesh and spirit, fight
sections.pass_a: This is the doctrine of Bellarmine on the grace of the first man, sole book, chap. 4. Where this is his fourth proposition, That rectitude with which Adam was created, and without which after his fall all men are born, was a supernatural gift. Which proposition in order to explain, he observes first that man naturally consists of flesh and spirit, and therefore shares nature partly with the beasts, partly with the Angels: and indeed by reason of the flesh and communion with the beasts, has a certain propensity toward corporal and sensible good, to which he is borne through sense and appetite: but by reason of the spirit and communion with the Angels, has a propensity toward spiritual and intelligible good, to which he is borne through intelligence and will. But from these diverse or contrary propensities there arises in one and the same man a certain fight, and from that fight a huge difficulty of acting well, while one propensity impedes the other.
pass_b: This is what Bellarmine teaches in chapter 4 of his single book On the Grace of the First Man. His fourth proposition there reads: "The rectitude with which Adam was created, and without which all men have been born since his fall, was a supernatural gift."

To explain it, he first notes that by nature man is made of flesh and spirit, and so shares a nature partly with the beasts and partly with the angels. Because of the flesh, which he shares with the beasts, he has a leaning toward bodily, sensible good, which he pursues through sense and appetite. Because of the spirit, which he shares with the angels, he has a leaning toward spiritual, intelligible good, which he pursues through understanding and will.
From these different, even opposed, leanings a kind of conflict arises within one and the same man, and from that conflict a great difficulty in doing good, as one leaning hinders the other.

choices.why: Bellarmine's propensio is a natural inclination, not yet a sinful desire; 'leaning' keeps it morally neutral.

notes: Robert Bellarmine, De gratia primi hominis (one book, part of his Controversies), chapter 4.

sections.title: Bellarmine: original righteousness a golden bridle; natural as from birth and as suiting nature, not as flowing from its principles
sections.pass_a: Then he says that divine providence at the beginning of creation, in order to apply a remedy to this disease or languor of human nature, which arose from the condition of matter, added to man a certain distinguished gift, namely Original justice, by which as by a certain golden bridle the lower part was held easily subject to the higher part, and the higher part to God. But the flesh was so subject to the spirit, that it could not be moved against its will, nor become rebellious to it, unless it itself became rebellious to God; yet it was in the power of the spirit to become rebellious to God, and not to become. Whence he gathers that the justice of the first man was indeed natural, insofar as natural is said of everything which is had from birth, and insofar as natural is said of that which is agreeable to nature, but was not natural, insofar as natural is distinguished from supernatural, and signifies that which flows from the principles of nature.
pass_b: Next he says that at the beginning of creation divine providence, to remedy this sickness or weakness of human nature arising from the condition of matter, gave man a remarkable gift, original righteousness. By it, as by a golden bridle, the lower part was kept easily subject to the higher, and the higher to God.

The flesh was so subject to the spirit that it could not be moved against the spirit's will or rebel against it unless the spirit itself rebelled against God, though it was in the spirit's power to rebel against God or not.

From this he concludes that the first man's righteousness was natural in the sense that whatever one has from birth is natural, and in the sense that what suits nature is natural; but it was not natural in the sense in which natural is distinguished from supernatural and means what flows from nature's principles.

choices.why: Ipso refers to the spirit; the English names it so the subject is clear.

sections.title: Bellarmine quoted: opponents call rectitude natural like health; Rome calls it supernatural in itself, so fallen man differs from pure-natural man as the stripped from the naked
sections.pass_a: The Adversaries, he says, think that that rectitude in which Adam was created was natural to him in this last way (namely insofar as natural is opposed to supernatural) namely because it was as it were a certain health owed to nature, and apt to be born from nature itself well constituted, that is, not corrupt: and now to men who lost that rectitude in Adam, some natural good is lacking, such as would be lacking to a beast, if it were born blind, or lame, or feverish. And now, if that original justice were divinely restored to some man, they would say it is a supernatural gift per accidens, not per se, as we said of eyes restored to the man born blind. But we think that that rectitude, even of the lower part, was a supernatural gift, and indeed per se, not per accidens, so that it neither flowed from the principles of nature, nor could flow. And because that gift was supernatural, as we shall prove at once, when it was removed, human nature left to itself began to experience that fight of the lower part with the higher, which was going to be natural, that is, to follow from the condition of matter, unless God had added the gift of justice to man. Wherefore the state of man after Adam's fall differs no more from the state of the same in pure naturals, than the despoiled differs from the naked: nor is human nature worse, if you take away original guilt, nor does it labor more with ignorance and infirmity, than it would be and labor if founded in pure naturals. Therefore the corruption of nature flowed not from the lack of some natural gift, nor from the accession of some bad quality, but from the sole loss of the supernatural gift on account of Adam's sin. Which opinion he proves to be common to the Scholastic Doctors old and more recent, with many testimonies of theirs afterwards brought forward.
pass_b: "Our opponents," Bellarmine says, "hold that the rectitude in which Adam was created was natural to him in this last sense, that is, as natural is opposed to supernatural. They hold it was a kind of health owed to nature and fitted to arise from nature itself when well formed, that is, uncorrupted. Men who lost that rectitude in Adam now lack some natural good, they say, as a beast would lack one if it were born blind, lame or feverish. And if original righteousness were now restored by God to some man, they would call it a supernatural gift by circumstance, not in itself, as we said of the eyes given back to the man born blind.

"We, however, hold that this rectitude, even in the lower part, was a supernatural gift, and supernatural in itself, not by circumstance, so that it neither flowed nor could flow from nature's principles. And because that gift was supernatural, as we shall prove shortly, once it was taken away human nature, left to itself, began to feel the conflict of lower part against higher that would have been natural, that is, would have followed from the condition of matter, had God not added the gift of righteousness to man.

"So man's state after Adam's fall differs from his state in a purely natural condition no more than a man stripped differs from a man naked. Take away original guilt, and human nature is no worse, and suffers no more from ignorance and weakness, than it would be and would suffer if it had been made in a purely natural condition. The corruption of nature, then, came not from the lack of some natural gift, nor from the addition of some bad quality, but solely from the loss of the supernatural gift because of Adam's sin."
Bellarmine then proves that this is the common view of the scholastic teachers, old and more recent, by citing many of their testimonies.

lemmas.gloss: a man stripped from a man naked

choices.english: a man stripped ... a man naked
choices.why: Bellarmine's famous image; the English keeps both participles concrete.

notes: Bellarmine, De gratia primi hominis, chapter 5, summarized at length by Le Blanc.

sections.title: Roman doctors agree it was grace, but divide: some say it was somehow owed to innocent nature, since God could not create man bad or wretched
sections.pass_a: But although the Doctors of the Roman Church commonly agree today in this, that the justice and sanctity of man in the state of integrity and innocence was a certain supernatural gift, and grace properly so called and superadded to nature: yet among them there remains here a notable difference of opinions. For some of them so want the justice and sanctity of the first man to have been supernatural, and to have pertained to grace not to nature, that it was yet in some way owed to innocent nature. So that it was impossible that the first man be founded and created by God without such grace: because namely, this would have conflicted with divine goodness, justice, and wisdom. For otherwise it would have come about that God created man either bad, or wretched, or rather both. For he cannot not be bad and not wretched who neither knows God, nor loves him with pure and chaste love, as befits a rational creature: and in whom the bodily senses and appetite drag reason unwilling and resisting to these lower things, nor obey the commands and dictate of the mind, but rebel and riot against it. But it is contrary to divine goodness that he found man bad and a sinner, or at least wretched, without any fault of his own.
pass_b: Although the teachers of the Roman Church now generally agree that man's righteousness and holiness in the state of integrity and innocence was a supernatural gift, grace in the proper sense, added on top of nature, there is still a notable difference of opinion among them.

Some of them hold that the first man's righteousness and holiness was supernatural and belonged to grace rather than to nature, yet was in some way owed to innocent nature. On their view it was impossible for God to make and create the first man without such grace, since that would have been at odds with God's goodness, justice and wisdom. Otherwise God would have created man either bad or wretched, or rather both.

A creature that neither knows God nor loves him with a pure and chaste love, as befits a rational creature, cannot help being bad and wretched. So too one whose bodily senses and appetite drag an unwilling, resisting reason down to lower things, and who do not obey the mind's commands and direction but rebel and riot against it. And it is contrary to God's goodness to make a man bad and a sinner, or at least wretched, through no fault of his own.

choices.term: non potest non malus & non miser non esse
choices.english: cannot help being bad and wretched
choices.why: The Latin piles up negatives; the English gives the positive sense.
rejected: may be neither bad nor wretched

sections.title: On that view only a debt founded on merit conflicts with grace
sections.pass_a: Therefore they do not think that every debt conflicts with grace, but only that which is founded on good works and merits. Therefore although God, while he founds a rational creature, ought, his goodness and wisdom requiring it, to confer on it gifts, and furnish aids which are necessary for pursuing God with pure and chaste love, and leading a just, tranquil and blessed life, those gifts and aids nevertheless, in their mind, pertain not to nature, but to grace properly so called: because such gifts and aids are in no way owed to the merits of the creature, and the creature of itself is not sufficient for these, unless it be helped by God above nature.
pass_b: So they do not think that every kind of debt is at odds with grace, only a debt founded on good works and merits.

When God makes a rational creature, his goodness and wisdom require that he give it the gifts and supply the help it needs to love God with a pure and chaste love and to live a righteous, peaceful and blessed life. Even so, in their view, those gifts and that help belong not to nature but to grace in the proper sense, because they are in no way owed to the creature's merits, and the creature is not equal to them by itself unless God helps it beyond nature.

choices.why: The distinction is between a debt arising from God's own goodness and a debt earned by merit.

sections.title: This is the Jansenists' teaching in their short Catechism on grace: a rational creature without grace would be disordered
sections.pass_a: This is the doctrine of those who follow the doctrine and tenets of Jansenius, as can be seen in the brief Catechism which they published on grace. For there in the fourth chapter, after they asserted that the first man was created in a state of sanctity and justice, of knowledge and divine love, God at once forming nature and communicating grace, they teach that man could not have been created in another state: because God can make nothing which is not ordered: but a rational creature would be disordered, unless it were created in a state of grace. And they prove that this is so from this, that the essential order of an intellectual creature is that it tend to God as to its center, and its origin. But it cannot tend thither except through the aid which grace supplies. Whence it follows that such a creature would be outside its proper order, if, not yet corrupted by sin, it were deprived of grace.
pass_b: This is the teaching of those who follow the doctrine and positions of Jansenius, as can be seen in the short Catechism on grace they published.

In its fourth chapter, after stating that the first man was created in a state of holiness and righteousness, of knowledge and love of God, with God at once forming his nature and giving him grace, they teach that man could not have been created in any other state. God can make nothing that is not well ordered, and a rational creature would be disordered unless it were created in a state of grace.

They prove this from the claim that an intellectual creature's essential order is to tend toward God as toward its center and its source. It cannot tend there except by the help grace supplies. It follows that such a creature, if deprived of grace before it was corrupted by sin, would be outside its proper order.

choices.why: The argument turns on order and disorder; 'well ordered' keeps the contrast with inordinatam.

notes: The 'short Catechism on grace' is the Jansenist Catéchisme de la grâce (1650).

sections.title: Drawn from Jansenius' Augustinus: man could not be created in pure nature without grace; the grace of love was still grace though fitting
sections.pass_a: These things are taken from Jansenius himself who in the posthumous book, which is entitled Augustinus, at length gathers, proves, and amplifies the same doctrine out of Augustine. But chiefly in the first and second book on the state of pure nature, where by many arguments he confirms and shows that man could not have been created in the state of pure nature, without all grace: because by the powers of nature alone, even not corrupt, without the aid of grace helping nature, man cannot love God with any true love, and be made blessed by any contemplation and fruition of God whatsoever. And so if God were supposed to create man in the state of pure nature, without all grace, he would necessarily create him both bad and wretched: which wholly conflicts with the goodness and wisdom of God. And moreover he teaches that the grace of the love of God, in which the first man was created, retains the truest character of grace, although God bestows it on the innocent creature by no debt of justice, but out of fittingness to the infirmity of the creature, out of the law of his wisdom, and of his kindness, and sanctity, and mercy and proper rectitude, lest otherwise all sins, and its love flowing down into lower things, should be turned back upon God himself, who commanded it to bind its love to no one but God its principle and end. Which are the very words of Jansenius, book 1. on the state of nature, chap. 20. whose title is, How the good will, in which a rational creature must be founded, was grace.
pass_b: These points are taken from Jansenius himself, who in his posthumous book entitled Augustinus gathers this same teaching from Augustine at length, proves it and enlarges on it. He does so especially in the first and second books on the state of pure nature.

There he argues at length that man could not have been created in a state of pure nature without any grace at all. By the powers of nature alone, even uncorrupted nature, without the help of grace assisting nature, man cannot love God with any true love or be made blessed by any kind of contemplation and enjoyment of God. So if God were supposed to create man in a state of pure nature without any grace, he would necessarily create him both bad and wretched, which is wholly at odds with God's goodness and wisdom.

He teaches besides that the grace of love for God in which the first man was created keeps the full and true character of grace. God gives it to the innocent creature not as a debt of justice but because it befits the creature's weakness, and by the law of his own wisdom, kindness, holiness, mercy and rectitude. Otherwise all sins, and the creature's love spilling down into lower things, would be laid at God's own door, since he commanded it to bind its love to no one but God, its source and end.
These are Jansenius' own words, in book 1 On the State of Nature, chapter 20, whose title is "How the good will in which a rational creature must be made was grace."

choices.english: would be laid at God's own door
choices.why: Revolvere here is to throw responsibility back onto someone; the idiom carries that in English.

notes: Cornelius Jansenius, Augustinus (Louvain, 1640, posthumous), volume 2, De statu naturae purae, book 1, chapter 20.

sections.title: Jansenius: debts of fittingness do not conflict with grace; knowledge and love of God are still grace even for the innocent
sections.pass_a: For as can be seen in the same place, in his opinion, any debts whatsoever, or connaturalities, decencies, congruences and equities, which arise from other heads than from the right of the creature, do not conflict even with grace most properly so called. And therefore although nothing would have been more connatural to a creature made to the image of God, than that it be created with knowledge and love of God: and nothing more congruent, more decent and more equitable in respect of God, than that to a rational innocent creature, which is ordered to God as to its natural end, those things should be given which are necessary for attaining that end, and that God in a certain way owed this to himself, and his attributes: yet that knowledge and love of God, without which no creature can enjoy God, deserves to be called grace, even in respect of innocent creatures; both because it is owed to no merits of the creature, and because knowledge and love of this kind surpasses the powers of any created nature, unless it be helped by God above nature.
pass_b: As can be seen in the same place, Jansenius holds that grace, even in the strictest sense, is not contradicted by any kind of debt, whether called connaturality, seemliness, fittingness or equity, so long as it arises from some other source than the creature's own right.

Nothing could be more connatural to a creature made in God's image than to be created with knowledge and love of God. On God's side, nothing could be more fitting, seemly and equitable than that a rational, innocent creature, ordered to God as its natural end, should be given what it needs to reach that end; in a sense God owed this to himself and to his attributes.

Yet that knowledge and love of God, without which no creature can enjoy God, deserves to be called grace even with respect to innocent creatures. It is owed to no merit of the creature, and knowledge and love of that kind surpass the powers of any created nature unless God helps it beyond nature.

choices.why: Jansenius' list of non-strict debts; each term gets a distinct English word.

notes: 'Made in God's image' is Genesis 1:27; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: The commoner Roman view: original righteousness wholly unowed, so a state of pure nature was possible
sections.pass_a: But the more common opinion of the Doctors of the Roman School goes the other way. For they think that the justice and sanctity which was in the first man was not only a supernatural gift, and which pertained to nature not to grace [so the print; thesis XII has to grace not to nature]; but also something wholly unowed to human nature, though innocent and not yet sinful: so that nothing would conflict with divine wisdom, goodness, and justice if man were created without such justice. Whence it is that among the possible states of man they place the state of pure nature, or of man, as they speak, in pure naturals. In which state in their mind, man would be neither just, nor unjust: neither guilty of any sin nor also endowed with any grace.
pass_b: The more common view among the teachers of the Roman school goes another way. They hold that the righteousness and holiness of the first man was not only a supernatural gift, belonging to grace and not to nature, but also something wholly unowed to human nature, even innocent nature not yet sinful. So it would not have been at odds with God's wisdom, goodness and justice for man to be created without such righteousness.

That is why they count among man's possible states the state of pure nature, or, as they put it, of man in a purely natural condition. In that state, as they see it, man would be neither righteous nor unrighteous, neither guilty of any sin nor endowed with any grace.

choices.term: quod ad naturam non ad gratiam pertinebat
choices.english: belonging to grace and not to nature
choices.why: The print inverts the phrase of thesis XII (ad gratiam non ad naturam). A gift called supernatural in the same breath cannot belong to nature rather than grace, so Pass B follows the sense Le Blanc's argument requires and the note records the printed reading.
rejected: belonging to nature and not to grace
belonging (as the print has it) to nature and not to grace

notes: The 1675 print reads 'quod ad naturam non ad gratiam pertinebat' ('which belonged to nature, not to grace'). Thesis XII and the argument require 'ad gratiam non ad naturam', so the translation follows that sense and treats the printed order as a printer's inversion.

sections.title: Pure nature defined negatively: nothing added, good or bad, beyond what is owed
sections.pass_a: For as the said Jansenius reports and explains the mind of the Scholastics in this part, on the state of pure nature first book first chapter, according to them, pure nature is so called by negative purity, because namely, it has nothing superadded either good, or bad, which is not owed to it: so that it neither has sin, and the punishment that accompanies sin, nor any gift of grace surpassing nature.
pass_b: Jansenius, already mentioned, reports and explains the scholastics' view on this in book 1, chapter 1 of On the State of Pure Nature. On their account nature is called pure by a negative purity: nothing is added to it, good or bad, beyond what is owed to it. It has neither sin, nor the punishment that goes with sin, nor any gift of grace beyond nature.

choices.why: Pure here means 'lacking additions', not 'morally clean'; the English keeps 'negative' to signal that.

sections.title: Look at fallen nature without its guilt: pure nature differs as the naked from the stripped, negation from privation
sections.pass_a: But that it may be easily understood what a state of nature of this kind comprehends, they bid us look at fallen nature, in which whatever we find besides the guilt of sin, this they profess to pertain to pure nature. For their solemn Rule is that pure nature differs from fallen nature as the naked from the despoiled, who do not differ otherwise, except that this one has lost what the other never had: so that therefore pure nature stands as a negation, fallen as a privation.
pass_b: To make it easy to see what such a state of nature includes, they tell us to look at fallen nature: whatever we find in it apart from the guilt of sin, they say, belongs to pure nature.

Their set rule is that pure nature differs from fallen nature as the naked man differs from the man stripped. The two differ only in that the one has lost what the other never had. So pure nature is like a negation, fallen nature like a privation.

choices.why: Scholastic pair: a negation is simple absence, a privation is the loss of something due.

sections.title: So man in pure nature would lack any ordering to the vision of God, faith and charity, and the fight of flesh and spirit would be natural
sections.pass_a: Therefore when they teach that man can be created by God, with no sin at all preceding, in the state of pure nature, they mean that man in that case would be created without ordering to eternal blessedness, or the clear vision of God, and consequently would be founded without faith in the intellect, and without charity loving God. Moreover that repugnance of flesh and spirit, which we experience in ourselves, would be wholly natural to such a man. To such an extent that the merely natural order requires that God allow those two contrary appetites to clash with reciprocal motions, neither withdrawing his concurrence, nor by some superadded gift restraining the mutual fight and hostility.
pass_b: So when they teach that God could create man in a state of pure nature with no prior sin at all, they mean that man would then be created without any ordering to eternal blessedness, that is, to the clear vision of God, and so would be made without faith in his intellect and without charity loving God.

They mean too that the conflict of flesh and spirit we experience would be wholly natural to such a man. The merely natural order would even require God to let those two opposed appetites clash back and forth, neither withdrawing his concurrence nor checking their mutual conflict and hostility by any added gift.

choices.why: Scholastic term for God's general cooperation with creatures' acts; kept as the technical word.

sections.title: Pure-nature man would be as ignorant and weak as fallen man, and outwardly worse off, lacking Adam's tradition and the promise of Christ
sections.pass_a: And therefore as regards the inner powers of the soul, there would be as much ignorance in pure nature, and weakness of thinking, judging, and living well, and proneness to sinning, as we experience in fallen nature. But as regards external things, more. For besides that the sensible objects exciting concupiscence would be the same, the bad counsels and examples of wicked men would then provoke to evil more powerfully. For the knowledge of God and of the virtues which had been communicated to Adam, and the memory of God's promises and threats, and the remembrance of the former state and the past fall, and the promise of the coming Christ, with the hope of his redemption, which flowed by tradition from the head to the descendants; could mitigate the facility of sinning in fallen nature, so that in this part blindness, a more general corruption of morals, and proneness to sinning would seem likely to have been more inclined in pure nature.
pass_b: So with regard to the inner powers of the soul, there would be as much ignorance in pure nature, as much weakness in thinking, judging and living well, and as much proneness to sin, as we experience in fallen nature. With regard to outward things there would be more.

The sense objects that stir up desire would be the same, and besides that, the evil counsel and example of wicked men would then urge men to evil more strongly. For in fallen nature the ease of sinning could be softened by what had come down by tradition from the head of the race to his descendants: the knowledge of God and of the virtues that had been given to Adam, the memory of God's promises and threats, the recollection of the former state and of the fall, and the promise of the coming Christ with the hope of his redemption.
So on this score blindness, a more widespread corruption of morals, and the tendency to sin would apparently have been greater in pure nature.

lemmas.gloss: from the head of the race to his descendants

choices.english: the promise of the coming Christ
choices.why: Le Blanc means the first gospel promise handed down from Adam; 'the coming Christ' keeps the forward look.

notes: The promise of the coming Christ handed down from Adam alludes to Genesis 3:15; the print gives no reference. Thesis XXI continues the scholastics' account as reported by Jansenius.
